body: Friday, July 24 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed is heading into next week's FOMC meeting with rates on hold, but the conversation has shifted dramatically — odds of a rate hike surged this week as oil ripped higher. The 10Y yield at 4.66% is up 27 bps over four weeks; the 2Y at 4.37% (prior close) is up 26 bps. The curve is positively sloped at +34 bps — still flat by historical standards and little changed over four weeks — but with rising yields driven by supply-shock inflation rather than growth optimism, this is a stagflationary skew. VIX at ~18 reflects complacency that looks dangerously mispriced against the geopolitical backdrop.

New / Most Important: The US-Iran conflict reignited, driving WTI to 88.43 — up a stunning 23% in four weeks. This is the single most important macro variable right now. New Trump tariffs took effect on July 24. CBS, CNBC, and USA Today all flagged that a Fed rate hike is now being debated for the first time in this cycle — a structurally new development. Intel beat and raised but the Street isn't buying it. Cathie Wood added $50M of Tesla after its 15% drawdown. The Nasdaq 100 is down 3.9% over four weeks even as the S&P 500 ekes out +1.0% — a clear rotation away from mega-cap tech.

Playbook ✓: Oil supply shocks feeding into rate-hike repricing is textbook. The divergence between S&P (+1%) and Nasdaq (-3.9%) confirms the "AI On/AI Off" rotation narrative Barron's flagged. Gold at 4070 holding as a geopolitical hedge alongside rising yields is classic fear-bid behavior.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The potential pivot from rate cuts to rate hikes is structurally new and breaks the entire 2025-2026 consensus script. For 18 months, the market consensus has been anchored around "when and how fast does the Fed cut." Now the debate has flipped 180 degrees. This changes the capital flow calculus entirely — if the Fed hikes into an oil supply shock, it's a policy error of the Trichet 2011 variety. Dollar strength on this dynamic (the "flight to quality" Yahoo flagged) would crush EM and commodities ex-oil simultaneously, creating a vicious feedback loop. The carry trade — particularly JPY-funded — would accelerate rather than unwind, which is the opposite of what consensus positioning expects. This is the most important regime change risk in the global macro landscape right now.

Macro Stance: The ECB held rates at 2.25% on July 23, as expected, but the tone shifted hawkishly. Traders are now pricing a September rate hike as the reignited Iran conflict drives energy prices higher — Europe's perennial vulnerability. Eurozone resilience data and firmer inflation readings published July 24 reinforce the hawkish pivot case.

New / Most Important: The ECB's hold was accompanied by explicit deliberation over a rate rise, a structural U-turn from the easing path that dominated the first half of 2026. This is the ECB's nightmare scenario: an exogenous energy shock forcing tightening into an already fragile industrial economy. VW cut its sales forecast, citing "extremely challenging" conditions — the auto sector is being squeezed from both sides (demand weakness + input cost inflation). The parallel to 2011 and 2022 is uncomfortable: both times the ECB hiked into energy shocks, it was forced to reverse within months.

Playbook ✓: Energy-sensitive Europe underperforming on an oil shock is textbook. ECB holding while debating hikes mirrors the hawkish-hold template.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The speed of the pivot from "further easing expected" to "September hike firmly in play" is remarkable — this happened in roughly 3-4 weeks. European credit spreads and periphery sovereign debt are not yet reflecting this regime change, creating a potential dislocation. If the ECB actually hikes while the industrial economy is deteriorating (VW's warning is a leading indicator), European equities — particularly cyclicals and autos — face a double squeeze that consensus hasn't priced.

Macro Stance: The PBOC added the most liquidity to the economy in five months to aid growth (Bloomberg, [Jul 23]) and is set to roll over 500 billion yuan of MLF, extending support for a third straight month (BigGo Finance, [Jul 23]), while loan prime rates stay on hold for a 14th consecutive month (The Business Times, [Jul 20]) and the market eyes a rate-cut window near the end of the third quarter (BigGo Finance, [Jul 21]). This is quantity easing, not cheaper credit. The yuan weakened slightly on the fixing (BusinessToday Malaysia, [Jul 17]) and UOB sees an upside bias below 6.7820 (TMGM, [Jul 20]), while a bond rally shows weak economic sentiment before the Politburo (Bloomberg, [Jul 22]). Prices are the wrong mix: June CPI rose only 1% (chinadailyhk, [Jul 8]) while PPI climbed 4.1% (BigGo Finance, [Jul 8]) to a near four-year high that squeezes manufacturers (Reuters, [Jul 8]).

PMIs & Activity: The surveys and the hard data point in different directions. The June official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.3 and the non-manufacturing PMI to 50.2 (Reuters, [Jun 29]); the private gauge capped the strongest factory quarter since late 2020 (Reuters, [Jun 30]). July PMIs are not yet out. Second-quarter GDP growth weakened to 4.3%, below the official target range (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]); June industrial output rose 5.3% y/y and retail sales returned to growth (BusinessLine, [Jul 15]), but retail sales of consumer goods were up just 1.3% in the first half (Ecns.cn, [Jul 15]), the car market heads for its worst year since 2021 (CNBC, [Jul 20]) and the CPCA expects July NEV retail sales to dip to about 980,000 (CnEVPost, [Jul 23]). Exports carry the cycle, up 27% y/y in June (Reuters, [Jul 13]).

Credit Impulse: The aggregate and the household picture diverge. The finance minister cites over 17 trillion yuan in new loans in the first half (BigGo Finance, [Jul 22]), yet June new loans missed forecasts (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]), credit growth undershot as the PBOC flagged a "new normal" (Caixin, [Jul 16]) and household loans decreased by 366.8 billion yuan in the first half (36Kr, [Jul 17]). Reconciled, corporate and state-linked borrowing carries the total while households deleverage, which is why extra liquidity lifts bonds more than spending.

Property: Prices are stabilising at the top while the financing base erodes. June new home prices fell at a slower pace, though Reuters doubts a recovery ([Jul 14]), and first-tier prices extended a 4-month rebound (SCMP, [Jul 15]). But property investment slumped 18% y/y in January–June (The Standard, [Jul 15]) and land-sales revenue plunged over 30% in the first half (BigGo Finance, [Jul 22]). Regulators are tightening developer funding, curbing a loan structure used by distressed developers (Bloomberg, [Jul 22]) and offshore loans for local real estate companies (The Standard, [Jul 23]); Vanke completed extensions on its 2026 public bonds with new funding (Caixin, [Jul 23]), and Central China Real Estate is selling two Henan landmarks for $443 million (BigGo Finance, [Jul 23]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: China clings to austerity despite a sharper slowdown (Bloomberg, [Jul 22]): first-half fiscal revenue rose 4.7% (Reuters, [Jul 22]) on stamp duty that surged 90% (BigGo Finance, [Jul 22]), and the finance minister's roadmap is a 100 billion yuan programme (BigGo Finance, [Jul 22]). Traders look to the Politburo for cues on the growth commitment (Bloomberg, [Jul 23]), and a new green-energy five-year plan targets a 30% wind and solar share by 2030 (BigGo Finance, [Jul 23]). On trade, the US imposed new tariffs on 60 economies as China-US talks on reciprocal cuts advance (BigGo Finance, [Jul 23]), with Beijing seeking opinions on tariff cuts covering $30 billion of trade (Reuters, [Jul 23]); the White House accuses Moonshot AI of stealing US technology (Anadolu Ajansı, [Jul 23]) even as both sides plan AI talks in September (Reuters, [Jul 22]).

Markets & Flows: China stocks fell on tariff concerns (TradingView, [Jul 23]) as AI and chip shares extended their correction (The Economic Times, [Jul 23]). The AI trade has already paid: mutual funds swung to a $287 billion profit on the AI binge (Caixin, [Jul 23]) and are pivoting to tech while cutting Hong Kong holdings (SCMP, [Jul 23]), but quant hedge fund losses topping 20% have rattled wealthy investors (Disruption Banking, [Jul 23]). The bond market defies the global slump (Seeking Alpha, [Jul 23]), and emerging-market assets rallied on China's tech support (Bloomberg, [Jul 21]).

New / Most Important: Beijing met the new US tariffs and the slowdown in the same session with two incremental tools. The PBOC added the most liquidity in five months, a quantity signal that stops short of a rate cut, while Beijing opened consultation on reciprocal tariff cuts covering $30 billion of trade just as Washington's new tariffs on 60 economies took hold. Liquidity without cheaper credit and tariff relief on a sliver of trade will not turn household demand; with austerity intact, the Politburo is where any genuine demand support would have to come from.

Playbook ✓: Liquidity-led easing, yuan management and discounted crude from sanctioned producers remain the expected toolkit.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The tariff wave on 60 economies hits an economy whose 50.3 PMI already rests on exports, so displaced Chinese supply flows toward Europe and EM; the FT says China's assault on Europe's car market has barely begun ([Jul 22]), a direct risk to European autos. Asia's growth pulse is splitting along AI lines: Japan's factory output surged in July (Reuters, [Jul 23]) while India's private sector growth slumped to an over four-year low (Reuters, [Jul 23]). For commodities, an 18% property-investment slump and crude imports at the lowest in nearly a decade (Bloomberg, [Jul 13]) cap Chinese demand, a drag on iron ore and AUD that extra PBOC liquidity does not reverse.

Macro Stance: The BOJ is caught in a genuine policy trap. The yen hit a 40-year low this week even as Japanese interest rates sit at a 31-year high — a stunning dislocation that reflects the Fed-BOJ rate gap keeping the carry trade alive. The BOJ is expected to hold at next week's meeting per Nikkei sources, but a Reuters poll showed markets expect another hike by December.

New / Most Important: This week's cluster of headlines reveals a structurally new dynamic: the US is now directly pressing the BOJ on rate hikes, with intervention threats looming. This is geopolitical monetary policy — Washington using currency diplomacy to force Japan's hand. Bloomberg reported the BOJ is "open to faster rate-hike pace" as the weak yen re-ignites imported inflation via the oil shock. Japan imports nearly all its energy — WTI at 88+ with the yen at 40-year lows means Japanese energy costs in yen terms are at historic extremes. The BOJ's conundrum is that hiking faster risks killing the domestic economy and equity market while not hiking fast enough means imported inflation spirals. This is a no-win scenario that could trigger the carry trade unwind that global markets have been dreading — the question is timing, not whether.

Playbook ✓: Weak yen / strong Nikkei correlation holding. BOJ incrementalism continues.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: US diplomatic pressure on BOJ rate policy is a new variable. If the BOJ is forced into an accelerated hiking cycle to defend the yen, the $4+ trillion JPY carry trade faces a disorderly unwind. The fact that intervention talk has surfaced alongside direct US pressure suggests this could happen faster than the market's "gradual normalization" consensus implies.

Macro Stance: Australia is facing the mirror image of its 2022-23 hiking cycle — just when markets expected the tightening to be over, the US-Iran war and surging fuel costs have made a fourth rate hike the base case. The RBA is now "twice as likely to hike" per the Guardian, and traders are convinced after a jobs surge. AUD strengthened above 0.7000 on the hawkish stance.

New / Most Important: The RBA released a new community survey revealing Australians fundamentally misunderstand how interest rates work — a structural communication problem as the central bank debates further tightening. The political dimension is intensifying, with Labor's economic promises unraveling and the RBA accused of "wanting people to lose their jobs."  |  Playbook ✓: Commodity-linked AUD benefiting from firm commodity prices and China's heavy iron ore buying is textbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Australia hiking into a global supply shock while its housing market remains stretched is a fragility that consensus is underweighting. The strong labor market is keeping the RBA hawkish, but the oil pass-through into CPI creates a policy trap — hiking won't fix supply-driven inflation but will crush rate-sensitive household spending.

Macro Stance: The week ends with the inflation debate reframed around fuel. FXMAG modelled diesel at 9 or 10 zloty and inflation of the order of 10% in a prolonged Middle East conflict ([Jul 24]), Energetyka24.com says the energy shock is feeding inflation with the full effects still ahead ([Jul 24]) and CEO Magazyn argued the oil shock could stop Polish rate cuts altogether ([Jul 23]). That is the backdrop to Kotecki's statement that inflation is diverging from the NBP projection and that a September cut cannot yet be promised (pb.pl, [Jul 23]), after one Council hawk called the earlier cuts premature (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 21]); Crédit Agricole's 25 bp September cut to 3.50% (PAP Biznes, [Jul 20]) now looks like the optimistic end of the range. The real economy is the hawks' ally: Rzeczpospolita's "chwilo trwaj" reads the complete data set as solid growth ([Jul 24]), retail sales rose 6.2% y/y against a 5.2% consensus (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 22]), industrial production 7.6% (CEO Magazyn, [Jul 20]), ING BSK sees Q2 GDP near 3.8% y/y (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 22]) and unemployment fell in June (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 23]). Wages are the soft spot: June pay rose 5.9% y/y (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 20]) but growth has slowed to its lowest since 2021 (FOCUS ON Business, [Jul 23]). The broader European energy-shock dynamic argues for a long hold.

Markets: Friday's session was a rotation out of the week's winners: KGHM fell 3.97% while Orlen rose 2.62% (FXMAG, [Jul 24]), Pepco led the gainers and Modivo and PGE ended the week under pressure (Inwestycje.pl, [Jul 24]). Business Insider Polska says Orlen's shares surprised in their reaction to President Nawrocki's decision on the windfall tax ([Jul 24]). The card, with Thursday's closes, still records a very strong week for energy: Orlen 155.86 (+6.8% 1W, +23.8% 4W) and PGE 10.6 (+14.2% / +8.4%), against KGHM 302.0 (-0.3% / -8.3%), Dino 28.86 (-1.9% / -1.5%), CD Projekt 226.3 (-3.5% / +1.3%), Allegro 44.88 (+1.2% / +19.5%), LPP 20300 (+1.3% / +10.0%), PKO 107.22 (-0.7% / +2.9%) and Pekao 232.9 (-0.2% / +1.3%); EPOL closed at 40.78, up 0.3% on the week and 7.3% over four weeks. The bond market is the week's loser: yields rose sharply on Friday even as the euro stayed stable (Bankier.pl, [Jul 24]), with German and French bonds at historic highs ([Jul 24]), a day after the Treasury raised more than 11.2 billion zloty at a successful auction (Bankier.pl, [Jul 23]). The zloty is trying to rebound with the dollar and euro losing on Friday (Comparic.pl, [Jul 24]) though FXMAG asks whether USD/PLN is heading for new records ([Jul 24]); the card has USD/PLN 3.8051 (+0.7% 1W, +1.0% 4W) and EUR/PLN 4.3303 (+0.1% / +1.2%).

Fiscal & Politics: President Nawrocki sent the new windfall tax to the Constitutional Tribunal, so the budget will not see the 4 billion zloty it was counting on (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 24]). The same day the finance ministry confirmed advanced variants of a 60 000 zloty tax-free allowance (Polskie Radio 24, Farmer.pl, [Jul 24]), TVN24 reports "various variants" on the table ([Jul 24]) and Bankier quotes the government's "we will not win if we do not deliver this" ([Jul 24]). The arithmetic is unforgiving: State Treasury debt exceeds 2.1 trillion zloty (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 24]), xyz.pl marks the historic moment of debt passing 60% of GDP ([Jul 24]) after Eurostat's 61.6% (XYZ, [Jul 21]), and the ministry has already ruled out public-sector pay rises for several years (Super Biznes, [Jul 21]). Bolesta pushed back on earmarking 50% of ETS revenue for decarbonisation, saying the finance minister knows best where to invest (Bankier.pl, [Jul 24]), and the president renewed his bid for a referendum on EU climate policy (Notes From Poland, [Jul 24]).

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen is in the political crossfire: its deal opening the Polish market to Ukraine's Nova Post enraged the right as "anti-Polish economic sabotage" (Money.pl, Do Rzeczy, [Jul 24]), Onet calls a PiS deputy's claim of fuel sold to Ukraine at 3 zloty a manipulation ([Jul 24]) and the company explained again why its Ukrainian prices differ (Rzeczpospolita, Super Biznes, [Jul 24]). It also signed a critical-infrastructure agreement with the fire service after reports Russia could attack it (XYZ, [Jul 24]). KGHM's shares rose on its June data earlier in the week (INNPoland.pl, [Jul 24]) before Friday's drop. CD Projekt has set the date for presenting the third Witcher 3 expansion (CrypS.pl, [Jul 24]). Dino sued the head of the Konfederacja Pracy union, which Głos Wielkopolski calls an attempt to gag unions ([Jul 24]). Banks are tempting with lower mortgage rates but not instant credit (Bizblog.pl, [Jul 24]); the state has only begun counting free-credit cases where banks may earn no interest (Money.pl, [Jul 24]), and the signed CHF law also covers foreign borrowers (Wprost, [Jul 24]).

Geopolitics & Security: There is now a queue for Poland's MiG-29s beyond Ukraine (Forsal.pl, [Jul 24]), Poland will use Ukraine's war experience to modernise its army (The New Voice of Ukraine, [Jul 24]). Poland is bidding to host a Patriot factory though a rocket-motor shortage keeps output years away (Tech Times, [Jul 24]); Belarusian special forces remain at the Ukrainian border (Forsal.pl, [Jul 23]).

New / Most Important: The veto-by-tribunal is the week's development. Blocking the windfall tax removes 4 billion zloty from a budget whose debt just passed 2.1 trillion zloty and 60% of GDP, on the day the ministry confirmed it is costing a 60 000 zloty tax-free allowance. Bond yields rising sharply on Friday is the market's answer; Orlen rising on the same news is the equity market's. Those are the same trade from opposite sides: Orlen keeps the profit the state cannot tax.

Playbook ✓: Hawkish hold consistent with CEE central banks facing imported energy inflation; energy over banks and short duration remain the positions the week rewarded.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: A government promising tax relief into a 60%-of-GDP debt while its own windfall tax is blocked is fiscal loosening by default, yet EUR/PLN sits at 4.33 as if nothing happened; the yield move says the bond market has stopped waiting for the currency.

Macro Stance: South Korea's stock market boom was flagged by the Korea Economic Institute this week, driven by the semiconductor super-cycle and structural governance reforms.  |  New / Most Important: Korea is emerging as the EM exception — a net beneficiary of AI capex flows while most EM suffers from dollar strength and oil inflation. The WEF's call to "rethink the developed-emerging market divide" is partly a Korea story.  |  Playbook ✓: Semi-driven equity outperformance.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None today.

Narrative: Bearish: the Nasdaq 100 is down 3.9% over four weeks, the worst major US index, in the "AI On/AI Off" regime Barron's identified. A 10Y at 4.66% compresses long-duration multiples, and the market doubts AI capex turns into earnings at the application layer.

Reported: IBM cut its 2026 revenue outlook after a Q2 miss (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]) as mainframe sales plunged 42% (MLQ.ai, [Jul 23]). ServiceNow beat on subscription growth (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]) and analysts increased their forecasts (Benzinga, [Jul 23]). Infosys cut its revenue forecast as IT service demand remains muted (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Dell — raised guidance by $27 billion and the Street is still catching up (TIKR.com, [Jul 21]). Apple — Morgan Stanley raised its target even as Wall Street cuts Tesla (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tech CEOs, Huang and Nadella among them, publicly defended open-source AI on July 20 as Washington threatened a crackdown; restrictions would fragment the global AI ecosystem and could push capital toward non-US AI. The open question is whether this is 1999, overinvestment before a bust, or 1995, the early innings of a build-out.
Narrative: Mixed: the platforms are caught between strong engagement and a rising cost of capital as yields climb, and Meta is financing its AI buildout with multibillion-dollar debt deals.

Reported: Alphabet fell more than 6% on capex growth expectations despite an earnings beat (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]), as its cash burn raised alarm for Big Tech (Reuters, [Jul 23]). Comcast beat on Peacock and box office successes (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 23]). T-Mobile beat on premium plan growth (Quartz, [Jul 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Meta — analysts expect an earnings decline (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 22]), a low bar, while BofA raised its target on AI revenue potential (Investing.com, [Jul 20]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Meta funding AI capex with structured debt rather than free cash flow says AI investment now exceeds even mega-cap cash generation. The platforms are becoming a credit story masquerading as a tech story, and bond spreads may matter more than ad growth.

Narrative: Bullish: rising yields are NIM-positive, though a +34 bps curve, little changed over four weeks, is still too flat to add much. Volatility in rates and commodities favours market makers, with Virtu flagged for a "durable profit cycle."

Reported: Blackstone beat expectations in a strong Q2 (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]). BNP Paribas lifted its dividend as revenue and profit beat estimates (WSJ, [Jul 23]). Schwab beat as retail investors piled into the market (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 21]).
EPS Upside Watch: KeyCorp — analysts increased their forecasts after upbeat Q2 earnings (Benzinga, [Jul 22]). W.R. Berkley — its Q2 is making analysts raise price targets (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: American Express triggered a sell signal: if even affluent consumer credit is cracking while yields surge, the "resilient consumer" story has holes. Jamie Dimon's warning that the next credit crisis will be 'worse than people expect' (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 22]) points the same way.

Narrative: Bullish: WTI at 88.43, up 23% in four weeks on the US-Iran conflict, is the dominant macro story, and US drillers added rigs for a fourth straight week. Murphy USA has entered a favourable profit cycle on improving fuel margins.

Reported: TotalEnergies posted its strongest profit in nearly three years as the Iran war lifted oil prices (Reuters, [Jul 23]). Repsol set out a fresh $571 million buyback as earnings surged on higher crude (WSJ, [Jul 23]). Weatherford missed Q2 estimates on Middle East disruptions (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: ExxonMobil — higher oil prices could boost its second-quarter profits by $5 billion (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 18]). Chevron — screened as poised to beat Q2 earnings estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 20]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: This is a supply shock, not demand: India's private-sector growth slumped to an over four-year low in July and euro-zone banks are tightening credit. Supply-shock rallies self-correct through demand destruction, so refiners and midstream beat upstream, and Repsol sees refining margins staying high next year (Reuters, [Jul 23]).

Narrative: Mixed: Eaton and nVent are scaling revenue on the AI data-centre power build-out, the most durable industrial theme, while supply-chain providers cut 1,200+ jobs this week and fuel hits the airlines.

Reported: RTX surged on a massive earnings beat and raised guidance (ChartMill, [Jul 23]). Union Pacific posted record results and raised its outlook (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]). American Airlines cut its 2026 outlook as the fuel shock overwhelmed revenue gains (Reuters, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: GE Vernova — Guggenheim raised its target to $1,450 on the beat (Investing.com, [Jul 23]) as its gas turbine backlog climbs to 116 GW (Utility Dive, [Jul 23]). Honeywell — raised its profit outlook after the aerospace spin-off (BigGo Finance, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Industrials are a two-speed sector, but not where expected: AI power equipment booms and airlines bleed on fuel, yet railroad Union Pacific posts record results. ETF-level positioning misses the split, so active selection is essential.
Narrative: Bearish: gasoline pass-through from $88 oil will crimp discretionary spending within weeks, and the AmEx sell signal points to consumer headwinds at the premium end.

Reported: Tesla sank after an earnings miss as AI spending soars (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]). Tractor Supply cut its outlook as shoppers continue to pull back (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 23]). Deckers beat and raised guidance, but the shares slid 3.5% (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Ralph Lauren — Raymond James upgraded it on a stronger growth outlook ahead of earnings (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 21]). Restaurants — three restaurant stocks screen as likely to surpass Q2 expectations (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tesla is the sector bellwether for the wrong reason: it is worth 37 automakers combined yet ranks last among them in revenue (Business Model Analyst, [Jul 23]). As an AI and robotics sentiment proxy, its moves say little about actual consumer fundamentals.
Narrative: Bullish: staples gain from the defensive rotation as the Nasdaq sells off and yields rise, and the "turtle mode" Barron's described favours them over growth.
Reported: Albertsons plunged as it said weaker grocery spending will cut into sales and earnings (CNBC, [Jul 23]). Philip Morris beat estimates as organic sales rose 7.6% (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 22]).

EPS Upside Watch: Staples screen — three consumer staples stocks are positioned for earnings surprises (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 22]). The sector — XLP's future earnings outlook is tilting up (Trefis, [Jul 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Even groceries are feeling the pullback: Albertsons' warning on weaker grocery spending says the defensive label does not protect volumes when fuel squeezes budgets. The staples that work are pricing-power brands, not the sector as a whole.
Narrative: Bullish: Eli Lilly is in a buy zone to "ride the peptide wave," and AI drug discovery drove Twist Bioscience's surge, so AI plus biotech is generating real revenue.

Reported: Thermo Fisher smashed estimates and raised its 2026 outlook as a pharma spending surge lifted growth (finance.biggo.com, [Jul 23]). Edwards posted 13.6% sales growth and raised revenue guidance (MassDevice, [Jul 23]). Medpace soared 15% after beating estimates and raising guidance (TIKR.com, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: UnitedHealth — BofA raised its target to $512 on strong earnings (Investing.com, [Jul 20]). Agios — expected to beat earnings estimates ahead of its Q2 release (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Danaher's 11% post-earnings fall (TIKR.com, [Jul 22]) looked like a warning for life-science tools, yet Thermo Fisher raised its outlook on surging pharma spending and Medpace beat. The problem was Danaher's, not the sector's.

Narrative: Bullish: copper at 6.36 (up 4.7%) is bid as an AI data-centre and grid-capex metal and gold at 4070 (up 1.0%) holds, while USA Rare Earth's Serra Verde deal strengthens its mine-to-magnet strategy.

Reported: Freeport-McMoRan's Q2 profit beat, helped by rising prices for copper, the AI and grid metal (Reuters, [Jul 23]). Dow swung to a profit on higher prices as sales grew (WSJ, [Jul 23]). Newmont topped estimates with record free cash flow despite a 13% gold-price correction (Kitco, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Anglo American — shares jumped as it sharply cut its copper cost guidance (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 23]), widening margins on a grid and data-centre metal. Air Products — earnings are expected to grow (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold (up 1.0%) lags copper (up 4.7%) despite the war premium because copper's bid comes from AI data-centre and grid capex, not the war. If Iran tensions ease, gold's premium fades while copper's AI and grid demand remains, a peace trade with a structural floor.

Narrative: Bearish: a 10Y at 4.66% and rising is toxic for rate-sensitive REITs. Data-centre REITs remain the exception, while office and retail landlords face higher rates and secular demand decline.

Reported: Rexford posted a $500M loss, blaming write-downs (The Real Deal, [Jul 23]). AvalonBay and Equity Residential beat FFO estimates in Q2 (Multifamily Dive, [Jul 23]). Homebuilder NVR missed Q2 revenue estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: IGB REIT — HLIB raised its earnings forecasts after a strong Q2 (NST Online, [Jul 22]). Singapore REITs — analysts see 'positive surprises' in H1 earnings (The Business Times, [Jul 21]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Asian landlords are raising payouts despite global rates: Suntec Reit's H1 DPU rose 24.8% (The Business Times, [Jul 23]) and Keppel DC Reit's rose 11.3% (The Business Times, [Jul 23]). The sector call is about rates; the earnings call is about who can lift rents.

Narrative: Mixed: utilities sit between the traditional headwind of rising yields and the AI-driven power-demand tailwind, and the "grid to rack" build-out benefits utilities with data-centre exposure.
